a: Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian
t: Alexander the Great, in one sentence
p: The book opens with Alexander's conquest of Persia (334–331 BC), the start of Greek rule over Judea.
b:
Alexander III of Macedon (356–323 BC), son of Philip II, crossed into Asia in 334 BC and defeated Darius III at Issus (333) and Gaugamela (331). Judea passed from Persian to Greek rule without a fight. 1 Maccabees gives his whole career two sentences, because its subject is what came after him: the Greek kingdoms, and the Greek way of life that a party in Jerusalem would want to copy (1:11–15).

Daniel's visions tell the same history in symbols: the goat from the west with one great horn that shatters the ram of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:5–8, 20–21), and "a mighty king" whose kingdom is broken up "toward the four winds of heaven" (Daniel 11:3–4). Most scholars think 1 Maccabees and Daniel 7–12 come out of the same crisis; see the chapter page.

a: the land of Kittim
p: Kittim first meant Cyprus; by this time it could mean any western sea people. Here it is Macedonia.
b: Kittim (Greek Chettieim) is named among the sons of Javan, the Greeks, in Genesis 10:4, and took its name from Kition on Cyprus. Balaam's oracle sees "ships... from the coast of Kittim" (Numbers 24:24), and Daniel 11:30 uses the same phrase for the Roman fleet that turned Antiochus back from Egypt in 168 BC. 1 Maccabees calls Macedonia Kittim again at 8:5, and in the Dead Sea Scrolls the Kittim are the last enemy of God's people, probably the Romans. The name told a Jewish reader that this conqueror came from the far west of the known world.
orig: ἐκ τῆς γῆς Χεττιείμ (ek tēs gēs Chettieim), 'from the land of Kittim'

a: He had already been king over Greece
p: The Greek prōteron can mean that Alexander ruled Greece before Persia, or that he was the first king of the Greek empire.
b: The Greek says Alexander "became king in his place, prōteron over Greece." Read as an adverb, it means he had already been king over Greece (he inherited Macedonia's leadership of the Greek cities in 336 BC) before he took Darius's throne; that is how the Plain takes it. The KJV's "the first over Greece" and the Vulgate's qui primus regnavit in Graecia, "who first reigned in Greece," take it as "first": Alexander as the first king of the Greek empire whose years the book will count (1:10, "the kingdom of the Greeks"). Swete notes that Codex Venetus has proteros, "the first," which supports that reading. Both make sense, and the history fits either; the Plain keeps the adverb because Alexandrinus and Sinaiticus have it.
orig: καὶ ἐβασίλευσεν ἀντ᾽ αὐτοῦ πρότερον ἐπὶ τὴν Ἑλλάδα (kai ebasileusen ant' autou proteron epi tēn Hellada)

a: his heart swelled with pride
p: The phrase marks Alexander, like Antiochus after him, as one of the proud kings God brings down.
b: "His heart was lifted up" is the old phrase for a ruler who forgets God: the king of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:2, 5), Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 5:20), Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:16), and the goat of Daniel's vision, which "grew very great" until its horn was broken (Daniel 8:8). Moses warns Israel of the same danger (Deuteronomy 8:14). The words tie Alexander to Antiochus, who "spoke with great arrogance" (1:24) and whose "glory will go to dung and worms" (2:62). The book's first theme is set: the empires rise in pride and fall.
orig: καὶ ὑψώθη, καὶ ἐπήρθη ἡ καρδία αὐτοῦ (kai hypsōthē, kai epērthē hē kardia autou)

a: he divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive
p: He did not. Alexander died suddenly in 323 BC without naming an heir, and his generals fought for decades.
b:
Greek and Roman historians agree that Alexander died at Babylon in June 323 BC, after a short fever, with no grown heir. His generals (the "Successors") ruled at first in the name of his half-brother and his infant son, and fought each other for forty years before the empire settled into the kingdoms of the Ptolemies in Egypt, the Seleucids in Syria and Mesopotamia, and the Antigonids in Macedonia. So this verse conflicts with the history we know. A story that Alexander handed out his realm on his deathbed did circulate: it appears in the late Alexander Romance, and the historian Quintus Curtius mentions it as a report he does not believe (10.10.5).

The book's point lies elsewhere: from one proud king came many, "and evils multiplied" (1:9). Daniel 11:4 says the same in prophecy: his kingdom is divided "toward the four winds" but "not to his descendants."

a: his officers
p: The Greek paides means servants or boys; at a court it means the king's officers, the young nobles raised as his companions.
b: The KJV has "his servants." At the Macedonian court the paides basilikoi, the "royal pages," were sons of nobles brought up with the prince, and Alexander's generals were the men he grew up with. The verse's own words make the point: they were "brought up with him from his youth" (syntrophoi). Compare Rehoboam's young advisers, "the boys he had grown up with" (1 Kings 12:8).
orig: τοὺς παῖδας αὐτοῦ τοὺς ἐνδόξους τοὺς συνεκτρόφους αὐτοῦ (tous paidas autou tous endoxous tous synektrophous autou)

a: Alexander had reigned twelve years
p: Alexander reigned from 336 to 323 BC, about twelve and a half years. The book is exact here.
b: Philip II was murdered in 336 BC and Alexander died in June 323 BC. Counting his reign as twelve years agrees with the Greek historians (Arrian, Anabasis 7.28 gives twelve years and eight months). The book's dates from here on are counted in the Seleucid era; see the note at 1:10.

a: a sinful root
p: A root that grows a poisonous plant. The image echoes Deuteronomy and sets Antiochus against the 'shoot from Jesse.'
b: Moses warned, "Take care that no root is here among you that bears poison and wormwood", someone who turns away to other gods (Deuteronomy 29:18). Isaiah promised the opposite, "a shoot from the stump of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1, 10). Daniel calls the same king "a contemptible person" to whom royal honor had not been given (Daniel 11:21). The Codex Venetus reads anēr, "a man," for riza, "root" (Swete's apparatus), a plainer word that loses the image.
orig: ῥίζα ἁμαρτωλὸς (rhiza hamartōlos)

a: Antiochus Epiphanes
p: His title means 'God made manifest.' Some of his enemies punned it into Epimanes, 'the madman.'
b:
Antiochus IV (reigned 175–164 BC) was a younger son of Antiochus III, "the Great." After Rome defeated his father at Magnesia (190 BC), the peace that followed (agreed in 189 BC, ratified at Apamea in 188 BC) sent him to Rome as a hostage, as this verse says. His brother Seleucus IV exchanged him for his own son Demetrius, and when Seleucus was murdered in 175 BC, Antiochus seized the throne.

His coins call him Theos Epiphanēs, "God made manifest," the first Seleucid to put a claim to divinity on his coins. The Greek historian Polybius reports that some called him Epimanēs, "the madman," for his strange behavior (Histories 26.1). Daniel's "little horn" that speaks "great things" (Daniel 7:8; 8:9–12) is read by most scholars as Antiochus; on whether he is also a picture of a final Antichrist, see the chapter 6 page.

a: the year 137 of the kingdom of the Greeks
t: Counting years from the Seleucid kingdom
p: The year 137 is 175 BC. The book counts from the start of Seleucid rule in 312/311 BC.
b:
1 Maccabees dates events by the Seleucid era, which began when Seleucus I took Babylon. There were two ways of counting: the Macedonian, from autumn 312 BC, and the Babylonian, from spring 311 BC. Most scholars think 1 Maccabees uses the Macedonian count for the king's affairs and sometimes the Babylonian (with the Jewish year beginning in spring) for events in Judea, which is why some of its dates are debated by a year. The usual conversions for this part are:

137 = 175 BC (Antiochus becomes king); 143 = 169 BC (the Temple robbed, 1:20); 145 = 167 BC (the altar profaned, 1:54); 146 = 166 BC (Mattathias dies, 2:70); 147 = 165 BC (Antiochus goes east, 3:37); 148 = 164 BC (the Temple rededicated, 4:52).

a: renegades went out from Israel
p: The Greek huios paranomos, 'a lawless son,' stands for a Hebrew phrase like 'sons of belial,' worthless men.
b: Codex Alexandrinus has the singular, huios paranomos, a "son of lawlessness," used as a collective (the verb is plural); Sinaiticus and Venetus have the plural, huioi paranomoi. Either way it is a Hebrew idiom: the Septuagint uses paranomoi for the bene beliyya'al, "worthless men," of Deuteronomy 13:13, who say "let us go and serve other gods." The echo is deliberate. These men are "renegades" (the book's word again at 1:34; 10:61): Jews who left the law. The book names no names; 2 Maccabees 4:7–15 blames the high priest Jason, Onias's brother, who bought the priesthood from Antiochus.
orig: ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ Ἰσραὴλ υἱὸς παράνομος (exēlthen ex Israēl huios paranomos)

a: let us make a covenant with the nations around us
p: The renegades propose exactly what the law of Moses forbade: a covenant with the peoples of the land.
b: "Do not make a covenant with those who live in the land" (Exodus 34:12); "Do not make a covenant with them" (Deuteronomy 7:2). The reformers' argument, that separation from the nations had brought only trouble, turns Deuteronomy's logic upside down: there, the evils come from joining the nations (Deuteronomy 31:16–17). 1 Maccabees uses "covenant" for both sides: Mattathias will "walk in the covenant of our ancestors" (2:20), and the renegades "turned away from the holy covenant" (1:15).

a: They built a gymnasium in Jerusalem
p: The gymnasium was the school of Greek citizenship, where young men exercised naked and learned Greek ways.
b:
In a Greek city the gymnasium trained the sons of citizens in athletics, music and letters, and enrolled them as an elite (the ephebes). Athletes exercised naked, which is why circumcision became an embarrassment (1:15). 2 Maccabees 4:9–14 says Jason paid Antiochus for the right to build it "right under the citadel" and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch, and that priests left the altar to watch the games.

Many historians (Bickerman, Tcherikover, Hengel) see the reform as a bid by Jerusalem's elite to turn the city into a Greek polis, with civic and trade privileges; 1 Maccabees sees only apostasy. The Plain keeps the word "gymnasium" because it is the Greek word itself.
orig: γυμνάσιον (gymnasion)

a: They made foreskins for themselves
p: The Greek says 'they made foreskins for themselves': a surgery that disguised circumcision.
b: Ancient doctors describe an operation (epispasmos) that stretched the skin to hide circumcision; Josephus says the reformers hid their circumcision "so as to be Greeks even when unclothed" (Antiquities 12.241). Paul uses the technical verb when he tells a circumcised man not to undo it: "let him not be uncircumcised" (1 Corinthians 7:18, Greek mē epispasthō). Jubilees 15:33–34 condemns Jews who leave their sons uncircumcised. In the book's eyes this is the clearest sign of all: the covenant sign of Genesis 17 cut away in the flesh.
orig: ἐποίησαν ἑαυτοῖς ἀκροβυστίαν (epoiēsan heautois akrobystian), 'they made foreskin for themselves'

a: sold themselves to do evil
p: The phrase is used of Ahab and of the northern kingdom before its fall.
b: Elijah tells Ahab, "you sold yourself to do what the LORD sees as evil" (1 Kings 21:20), and Kings says the northern tribes "sold themselves to do evil in the LORD's eyes" before Assyria carried them off (2 Kings 17:17). The writer of 1 Maccabees often speaks in the language of Kings; here he sets the reformers beside Israel's worst apostates. "Yoked themselves" echoes Numbers 25:3, where Israel "yoked itself" to the Baal of Peor, the scene behind Phinehas's zeal (see 2:26).
orig: ἐζευγίσθησαν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, καὶ ἐπράθησαν ποιῆσαι πονηρόν (ezeugisthēsan tois ethnesin, kai eprathēsan poiēsai ponēron)

a: Antiochus planned to become king of the land of Egypt too
p: Antiochus invaded Egypt in 170–169 and again in 168 BC. Rome stopped him with a famous line in the sand.
b:
The boy king Ptolemy VI's advisers had planned to retake Coele-Syria; Antiochus struck first, won at Pelusium, and took most of Egypt except Alexandria (170–169 BC). This verse and 1:17–19 describe that first campaign. When he came back in 168 BC, a Roman envoy, Gaius Popilius Laenas, met him outside Alexandria, drew a circle around him in the sand and demanded an answer before he stepped out of it. Antiochus withdrew (Polybius, Histories 29.27).

Daniel tells both campaigns: the king of the north wins the first time (Daniel 11:25–28), but the second time "ships of Kittim" come against him and "he will lose heart and return" and rage against "the holy covenant" (Daniel 11:29–30). 1 Maccabees does not mention Rome's humiliation of Antiochus.

a: in the year 143
p: 1 Maccabees puts the Temple robbery in 169 BC; 2 Maccabees adds a bloody punishment of Jerusalem after a revolt.
b: The year 143 is 169 BC, after the first Egyptian campaign. 2 Maccabees 5:1–21 tells a fuller story: a false rumor of Antiochus's death let the deposed high priest Jason attack Jerusalem; Antiochus took this as revolt, killed many, and robbed the Temple with Menelaus as his guide, carrying off 1,800 talents. Historians debate whether the two books describe one visit (169 BC) or two (169 and 168 BC). Daniel 11:28 has the king return from Egypt "with great wealth, his heart set against the holy covenant."

a: He took away the gold altar and the lampstand that gave light
t: The furniture of the holy place
p: The list follows the furnishings of the holy place: incense altar, lampstand, table, vessels and curtain.
b: These are the furnishings of the holy place that Exodus describes for the tabernacle: the gold altar for incense (Exodus 30:1–10), the lampstand (Exodus 25:31–40), the table of the Presence Bread with its dishes and pitchers (Exodus 25:23–30), and the curtain (Exodus 26:31–33). Babylon had carried off Solomon's vessels (2 Kings 25:13–15); these were the replacements of the Second Temple. The list prepares for 4:49–51, where Judas's priests make new ones and set the same things back in order.

a: He scraped it all off
p: The Greek elepisen means 'peeled' or 'stripped the scales off': he scraped away the gold plating.
b: The verb lepizō is used for peeling bark or scaling fish. Antiochus did not only carry off loose vessels; he stripped the gold leaf from the Temple's façade. Swete notes that the second letter e of the verb in Alexandrinus stands on an erasure. Compare Hezekiah, who stripped the gold from the Temple doors to pay Sennacherib (2 Kings 18:16).
orig: καὶ ἐλέπισεν πάντα (kai elepisen panta)

a: And they committed a massacre and spoke with great arrogance
p: Daniel's little horn has 'a mouth that spoke great things.' The book uses the same language for Antiochus.
b: The arrogant mouth is Daniel's mark of the king who defies God: "a mouth speaking great things" (Daniel 7:8, 20), "he will speak words against the Most High" (Daniel 7:25), "he will speak astonishing things against the God of gods" (Daniel 11:36). Revelation gives the beast the same mouth (Revelation 13:5). On who did the killing, see the variant: Alexandrinus makes it "they," his men; the other codices and the KJV make it Antiochus.

a: Great mourning came upon Israel
p: The book breaks into poetry five times in chapters 1–3, each in the style of Lamentations and the Psalms.
b: The poems at 1:25–28, 1:36–40, 2:7–13, 3:3–9 and 3:45 are written in Hebrew-style parallel lines. Most scholars think 1 Maccabees was written in Hebrew and translated into Greek; these poems read like the laments for Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC (Lamentations 1–2; Psalms 74 and 79). The rulers who groan, the young women and men who faint, and the bride in her room recall Lamentations 1:4 and 2:10, 21, and Joel's call for the bridegroom to leave his room (Joel 2:16).

a: an officer to collect tribute
t: The tax officer, or the Mysian commander?
p: 2 Maccabees names him Apollonius, 'the Mysarch.' A Hebrew wordplay may explain the two titles.
b: 2 Maccabees 5:24–26 says Antiochus sent Apollonius "the Mysarch," commander of Mysian mercenaries, with 22,000 men, who waited for the Sabbath and then attacked. Many scholars think the Hebrew behind 1 Maccabees read sar ha-missim, "chief of tribute," and that the translator misread or reinterpreted sar ha-musim, "chief of the Mysians," or the reverse. This is a guess about a lost Hebrew text, but it would explain why one book has a tax collector and the other a mercenary general. Daniel 11:20 calls an earlier Seleucid "one who sends a tax collector through the glory of the kingdom."
orig: ἄρχοντα φορολογίας (archonta phorologias), 'a ruler of tribute'

a: it became their Citadel
p: A Seleucid fortress in Jerusalem that held out for 25 years, until Simon took it in 141 BC (13:49–52).
b: The Greek akra means "height, citadel." Garrisoned by Seleucid troops and Jewish renegades, it overlooked the Temple and was a thorn in Judea's side through all the wars of Judas and Jonathan (4:41; 6:18–27; 11:20–21), until Simon starved it into surrender (13:49–52). Its location is debated: the text says "the City of David," south of the Temple. In 2015 archaeologists working in the Givati parking lot, in the City of David, reported a massive wall, tower and glacis that they identified as the Akra; others still place it nearer the Temple Mount.
orig: εἰς ἄκραν (eis akran)

a: an evil adversary to Israel at all times
p: The Greek diabolos, 'slanderer, adversary,' is the Septuagint word for the satan.
b: In the Septuagint diabolos translates Hebrew satan, "accuser, adversary" (Job 1:6; Zechariah 3:1; 1 Chronicles 21:1), and in the New Testament it is the devil. Here it is used of a fortress, as the Hebrew satan could be used of any human adversary (1 Kings 11:14, 23). The Plain gives "adversary" so as not to turn a garrison into a demon; but a Greek reader would hear the overtone.
orig: εἰς διάβολον πονηρὸν (eis diabolon ponēron)

a: her feasts were turned into mourning
p: The line borrows Amos's threat against Israel, now fulfilled by a foreign king.
b: Amos had warned, "I will turn your feasts into mourning" (Amos 8:10), and Lamentations says the LORD made Zion forget "feast and Sabbath" (Lamentations 2:6). The book uses these words of its own day. Tobit quotes Amos 8:10 at the death of a neighbor (Tobit 2:6). 2 Maccabees 6:6 says that in these years it "was not allowed to keep the Sabbath, or to guard the feasts of the fathers."

a: all were to be one people
t: Did Antiochus order the whole empire to give up its customs?
p: No other source reports an empire-wide decree. Most historians think the ban fell on Judea alone.
b:
The book says the decree went to "his whole kingdom" and that "all the nations accepted" (1:42). No Greek or Babylonian source mentions such a decree, and the Seleucid empire stayed as varied as before. Most historians think the persecution was aimed at Judea, though perhaps framed as a call to unity. Why Antiochus did it is debated: Bickerman blamed the Jewish reformers around Menelaus, who wanted a Judaism without the law; Tcherikover saw it as punishment for a revolt; others stress the king's need for money and loyalty.

Daniel says the king "will plan to change times and law" (Daniel 7:25). On the reliability of the book's history overall, see the book's opening pages.

a: Many even from Israel were glad to take up his worship
p: The book never hides that many Jews went along. The war was also a war among Jews.
b: From 1:11 to 1:52 the book keeps returning to Jews who chose the king's ways: the renegades, "many even from Israel," "everyone who was abandoning the law." Mattathias's first blow falls on a Jew (2:24), and his army strikes "sinners" and "lawless men" (2:44), that is, Jews. Daniel draws the same line: "those who act wickedly toward the covenant" against "the people who know their God" (Daniel 11:32). Readers have long seen the revolt as both a war of liberation and a civil war over what it means to be Israel.

a: the holy ones
p: The Greek hagious is masculine: holy people, probably the priests, or Israel itself.
b: The KJV reads "the holy people," the Douay "the holy people" too. The form hagious is masculine plural, so it means persons, not "holy things" (which would be hagia). Most take it as the priests, or as the faithful of Israel, called "the holy ones" (Daniel 7:21–22, 25; 8:24). The decree aims at both the place and the people set apart.
orig: καὶ μιᾶναι ἁγίασμα καὶ ἁγίους (kai miānai hagiasma kai hagious)

a: to sacrifice pigs and unclean animals
p: The Greek koina means 'common,' the word Peter uses when he says he has never eaten anything common or unclean.
b: Pig is the clearest of the forbidden animals (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8; Isaiah 65:4; 66:17). The Greek calls the others ktēnē koina, "common animals," meaning ritually profane. The same word is used at 1:62 ("what was unclean," koina), and later in the New Testament: Peter says "I have never eaten anything common or unclean" (Acts 10:14), and Mark speaks of eating with "common," that is unwashed, hands (Mark 7:2). Sinaiticus as first written has polla, "many," here.
orig: θύειν ὕεια καὶ κτήνη κοινά (thyein hyeia kai ktēnē koina)

a: so that they would forget the law and change all its rules
p: Daniel foresaw a king who would 'plan to change times and law.' This is the event most scholars think he meant.
b: Daniel 7:25 says the fourth beast's little horn "will speak words against the Most High, wear out the holy ones of the Most High, and plan to change times and law." The decree here bans the calendar of Sabbaths and feasts (1:45) and the law itself (1:49, 56–57). Critical scholars read Daniel 7–12 as written during this crisis; many traditional Christian readers hold that Daniel foretold it centuries before and that its words look beyond it as well.

a: On the fifteenth day of Kislev, in the year 145
p: Kislev is the ninth month (November-December). The year 145 is 167 BC.
b: Kislev (Greek Chaseleu, KJV "Casleu") is the ninth month of the Jewish year, counted from spring (Nehemiah 1:1; Zechariah 7:1). The fifteenth of Kislev in 167 BC fell in December. Ten days later, on the 25th, the first pagan sacrifice was offered (1:59), and exactly three years later, on the 25th of Kislev, 148, Judas rededicated the altar (4:52–54). Hanukkah still begins on 25 Kislev.

a: they built an abomination of desolation on the altar
p: The phrase is Daniel's. Most think it was a pagan altar or cult object built on top of the altar of burnt offering.
b:
The Greek bdelygma erēmōseōs is the Septuagint's phrase in Daniel 11:31 and 12:11 for the Hebrew shiqquts (me)shomem, "the abomination that desolates" (compare Daniel 9:27; 8:13). Shiqquts, "detestable thing," is the Bible's sneering word for an idol (1 Kings 11:5, 7). Since Eberhard Nestle (1884), many scholars have heard a pun: shomem "desolating" mocks Shamem, as in Ba'al Shamem, "Lord of Heaven," the Syrian name for the god the Greeks called Olympian Zeus, to whom 2 Maccabees 6:2 says the Temple was dedicated.

The verb is "built" (ōkodomēsan), and 1:59 speaks of the pagan altar "that stood on top of the altar"; so most take it as an altar, perhaps with sacred stones. The Vulgate, read for centuries in the West, calls it abominandum idolum desolationis, "the abominable idol of desolation" (Vulgate 1:57), and says the king himself set it up. Jesus' warning about "the abomination of desolation" standing in the holy place (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14) takes up Daniel's words; see the card on this page.
orig: ᾠκοδόμησαν βδέλυγμα ἐρημώσεως ἐπὶ τὸ θυσιαστήριον (ōkodomēsan bdelygma erēmōseōs epi to thysiastērion)
r: Daniel 11:31; Daniel 12:11; Daniel 9:27; Daniel 8:13; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14; 2 Maccabees 6:2–5

a: Any scrolls of the law they found, they ripped apart and burned
p: The first recorded attempt to destroy the books of Israel's law.
b: King Jehoiakim had cut up Jeremiah's scroll and burned it in his brazier (Jeremiah 36:23), but that was one prophet's scroll. Here the target is "the law" and every "scroll of the covenant" (1:57), the first known attempt to wipe out the books of a people's faith. The scene explains why 3:48 makes so much of the scroll of the law spread out at Mizpah. Josephus says the king's men left no copy they found (Antiquities 12.256).

a: On the twenty-fifth day of the month they offered sacrifice
p: 2 Maccabees says the people were forced to share in a monthly sacrifice on the king's birthday.
b: 2 Maccabees 6:7 says that "Each month, on the king's birthday," Jews were made to eat the sacrifices, and at the festival of Dionysus to carry ivy. Many scholars think the 25th of each month was that monthly birthday feast, which would explain "month after month" in 1:58. The date also matters for Hanukkah: the altar was rededicated on the same day of the month it had been first profaned (4:54).

a: the pagan altar that stood on top of the altar of sacrifice
p: The book uses bōmos for a pagan altar and thysiastērion for the LORD's altar, like the Septuagint.
b: The Septuagint keeps thysiastērion for Israel's altar and uses bōmos, the ordinary Greek word, mostly for pagan altars (Numbers 23:1; Hosea 10:8; Isaiah 15:2). 1 Maccabees follows the rule: the abomination was built "on the altar" (thysiastērion, 1:54), but the sacrifice was offered "on the bōmos that was on the thysiastērion." Mattathias tears down a bōmos at Modein (2:25) and his men tear down the bōmoi in the towns (2:45). The Douay calls it "the altar of the idol that was over against the altar of God."
orig: ἐπὶ τὸν βωμὸν ὃς ἦν ἐπὶ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου (epi ton bōmon hos ēn epi tou thysiastēriou)

a: They hung the babies from their mothers' necks
p: 2 Maccabees tells of two mothers led around the city with their babies hung at their breasts, then thrown from the wall.
b: 2 Maccabees 6:10 tells of two women who had circumcised their sons and were paraded through Jerusalem with the babies hanging at their breasts before being thrown down from the wall. 4 Maccabees and later Jewish and Christian tradition kept the memory of such mothers. Alexandrinus has no verb for the families and the circumcisers. They may go with "they hung," as the Plain takes them, or with "they put to death" in 1:60, so that the families were killed and only the babies hung. A corrector of Sinaiticus and the KJV supply "plundered" and "killed" (see the variant).

a: steeled themselves not to eat what was unclean
p: Those who would not eat became the models for the martyr stories of 2 and 4 Maccabees, and for Hebrews 11.
b:
Daniel had already "made up his mind not to defile himself" with the king's food (Daniel 1:8). Here refusing food costs life. 2 Maccabees 6:18–7:42 tells the deaths of the old scribe Eleazar and of a mother and her seven sons, who would not eat pork; 4 Maccabees retells them as proof that reason can master suffering. Hebrews 11:35–38 probably remembers them: "others were tortured, not accepting release, so that they might gain a better resurrection."

Christians from the fourth century on honored these martyrs; the Orthodox churches keep a feast of the Holy Maccabees on 1 August, and the Roman Martyrology commemorates them that day (until 1969 it was also a feast of the General Roman Calendar). On the food laws themselves for Christians, see the card at Leviticus 11.

a: And a very great wrath fell on Israel
p: The book does not say. Most take it as God's anger at Israel's sin; some as the king's fury.
b: Like 2 Kings 3:27, the verse says only that "wrath" came. Most readers take it as God's anger, as in Daniel's "period of wrath" (Daniel 8:19; 11:36) and 2 Maccabees 5:17–20; 7:32–38, where the persecution is the discipline of a God "angry for a little while" at his people's sins, and the martyrs' deaths help bring it to an end. Others read it as the king's rage, carried out on Israel. 1 Maccabees, which never names God, leaves it open; Judas "turned anger away from Israel" (3:8).

a: a priest of the line of Joarib
t: A priest of the first course
p: Joarib is Jehoiarib, the first of the twenty-four priestly families in 1 Chronicles 24:7.
b: When David's priests were divided into twenty-four courses that served in turn, "the first lot came out for Jehoiarib" (1 Chronicles 24:7). Joarib (Greek Iōareim; Venetus spells it Iōareib) is the same name. The family was a priestly one of the highest rank, but not of the high priestly line of Zadok and Onias. That matters later, when Mattathias's sons take the high priesthood (10:20–21; 14:41). Josephus adds that Mattathias was a great-grandson of one Asamonaios, the name behind "Hasmonean" (Antiquities 12.265); 1 Maccabees never uses the family name.

a: he made his home in Modein
p: A village in the foothills northwest of Jerusalem, near today's city of Modi'in.
b: Modein (Greek Mōdeein; Hebrew Modi'im) lay about 17 miles northwest of Jerusalem, where the hills come down to the coastal plain. The family's tombs were there; Simon later built a great monument over them that could be seen from the sea (13:25–30). "He came from Jerusalem" may mean that the family moved out when the city was taken over (1:38), or simply that they were Jerusalem priests by origin. The site is usually placed near the modern city of Modi'in, though which ruin it is remains debated.

a: Judas, called Maccabeus
p: The nickname probably comes from Hebrew maqqabah, 'hammer.' Other explanations have been proposed.
b: Each son has a nickname whose meaning is mostly lost: Gaddi, Thassi, Avaran, Apphus. Judas's is the one that stuck, and gave its name to the books and to the whole family (the Maccabees). The most common explanation takes it from Hebrew maqqabah or Aramaic maqqaba, "hammer" (Judges 4:21; Isaiah 44:12), for his blows against the enemy. Others have suggested "designated by the LORD" (from naqab, "name, designate") or a word for the shape of his head. The Latin form Maccabaeus became the name for the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7 as well, though they were not of this family.
orig: Ἰούδας ὁ καλούμενος Μακκαβαῖος (Ioudas ho kaloumenos Makkabaios)

a: Woe is me! Why was I born to see this
p: Mattathias speaks like Jeremiah and the poets of Lamentations over the fall of Jerusalem.
b: Jeremiah cursed the day he was born to see "trouble and grief" (Jeremiah 20:18), and Rebekah asked "why am I alive?" (Genesis 25:22). The lament of 2:7–13 is built from Lamentations: the city once free now a slave (Lamentations 1:1), her infants in the streets (Lamentations 2:11, 19), her young men by the sword (Lamentations 2:21), her treasures taken by enemies (Lamentations 1:10). The Babylonian disaster is happening again; the question is what the faithful will do.
r: Jeremiah 20:18; Lamentations 1:1; Lamentations 1:10; Lamentations 2:11; Lamentations 2:21; Psalm 79:1

a: taken her palaces for its own
p: The Greek basileia can be 'palaces' or 'kingdom' depending on accent. The KJV has 'a part in her kingdom.'
b: Swete prints basíleia, the neuter plural "palaces, royal residences," which the Plain follows. With a different accent, basileía, the word means "kingdom, royal power," which is how the KJV ("had a part in her kingdom") and the Vulgate (regnum) read it. Ancient manuscripts had no accents, so this is a choice of editors. Either way the nations have taken over what belonged to Israel's kings.
orig: ἐκληρονόμησεν βασίλεια (eklēronomēsen basileia)

a: enforcing the apostasy
p: The Greek apostasia, 'revolt, falling away,' is the word Paul uses for the great falling away before the end.
b: In political Greek apostasia means "revolt"; in the Septuagint it means rebellion against God (Joshua 22:22; Jeremiah 2:19). Here the king's officers force people to fall away from the law. Paul writes that the day of the Lord will not come "unless the apostasy comes first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed... who sets himself in God's temple" (2 Thessalonians 2:3–4). Many interpreters, ancient and modern, have heard in Paul's words an echo of the Antiochus crisis: a forced apostasy and a ruler who claims divine honors in the Temple.
orig: οἱ καταναγκάζοντες τὴν ἀποστασίαν (hoi katanankazontes tēn apostasian)

a: the Friends of the King
p: 'Friend of the King' was a rank at the Seleucid court, given with purple robes and gifts.
b: Hellenistic kings had an order of honored courtiers called "Friends" (philoi), with higher grades such as "First Friends" and "Kinsmen" (10:65; 10:89; 11:27). Being enrolled among the Friends brought gifts, a purple robe and access to the king. The officers offer Mattathias a place among the king's elite in return for leading his town in sacrifice. His sons will later accept such titles from Seleucid kings (10:20, 65), one of the ironies the book records without comment.

a: yet I and my sons and my brothers will walk in the covenant of our ancestors
p: Mattathias's answer echoes Joshua's and the three young men's refusal before Nebuchadnezzar.
b: Joshua told Israel, "I and my family will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15). Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael told Nebuchadnezzar that even if God did not save them they would not serve his gods (Daniel 3:16–18), and Mattathias names them in his testament (2:59). "To the right or to the left" (2:22) is Moses' and Joshua's phrase for leaving the law (Deuteronomy 5:32; Joshua 1:7). The speech gives the revolt its creed: not freedom in general, but faithfulness to the covenant.

a: Never may we abandon the law and its rules!
p: The Greek hileōs hēmin, 'mercy on us,' is an oath-like way of saying 'God forbid.'
b: Hileōs hēmin means literally "(may he be) merciful to us," short for "God be merciful to us" if we do it. It renders Hebrew chalilah, "far be it," as in 2 Samuel 20:20 and 1 Chronicles 11:19 in the Septuagint, and Peter uses it in Matthew 16:22 ("Heaven spare you, Lord!"). The KJV's "God forbid" supplies God; the Plain keeps the book's habit of not naming him.
orig: ἵλεως ἡμῖν (hileōs hēmin)

a: His insides trembled
p: The Greek has 'kidneys,' the seat of deep feeling in Hebrew thought, as 'heart' is for us.
b: The KJV keeps "his reins trembled" ("reins" is old English for kidneys). In the Psalms and the prophets the kidneys are where God tests a person's inmost feelings (Psalm 7:9; Jeremiah 11:20; Revelation 2:23). The verse shows that Mattathias's act came from deep feeling under control, "as justice demanded": the Greek kata to krima can mean "according to the law's ruling," claiming that the killing was a lawful sentence and not a fit of rage (Exodus 22:20; Deuteronomy 13:6–9).
orig: καὶ ἐτρόμησαν οἱ νεφροὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἀνήνεγκεν θυμὸν κατὰ τὸ κρίμα (kai etromēsan hoi nephroi autou, kai anēnenken thymon kata to krima)

a: He ran and slaughtered the man on the altar
p: The book praises the killing as zeal like Phinehas's. Later readers have judged it in very different ways.
b:
1 Maccabees presents the deed as lawful zeal: Deuteronomy 13:6–10 orders the death of an Israelite who leads others to worship other gods, and Exodus 22:20 says "Anyone who sacrifices to the gods, and not to the LORD alone, is to be put under the ban and destroyed." The man was killed "on the altar," his own sacrifice turned against him.

Later readers divide. Jewish tradition honors Mattathias in the Hanukkah prayer Al ha-Nissim, but the rabbis also limited zealous killing to the act itself and would not let a court authorize it (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6; Babylonian Talmud Sanhedrin 82a). The Zealots of the first century AD claimed Phinehas and Mattathias as models (Hengel). Christian readers have praised Mattathias's courage while asking whether Christ's way allows such force (Matthew 26:52; John 18:36). John J. Collins has argued that the Phinehas tradition shows how Scripture can be used to make violence seem holy. On when believers may resist a ruler by force, see the 1 Samuel 24 card.

a: as Phinehas had been against Zimri son of Salu
p: The book explicitly models Mattathias on Phinehas, the priest whose spear stopped the plague at Peor (Numbers 25).
b:
When an Israelite brought a Midianite woman into the camp at Peor, Phinehas "took a spear in his hand" and killed both, and "the plague on the Israelites was held back." God gave him "my covenant: peace... a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he was zealous for his God and made atonement for the Israelites" (Numbers 25:7–13). The parallels are close: a priest, a public act of apostasy, a killing, and a covenant of priesthood as reward (2:54). Psalm 106 says of Phinehas, "It was reckoned to him as righteousness" (Psalm 106:31).

The man Phinehas killed was "Zimri son of Salu" (Numbers 25:14); the Greek here has Zambri son of Salōm. The comparison also hints at the book's purpose: the Hasmoneans, a priestly family not of Zadok's line, held the high priesthood, and Phinehas's covenant justified a zealous priest's claim to it (see 14:41).

a: Everyone who is zealous for the law and stands by the covenant, come out and follow me!
p: The cry recalls Moses at the golden calf, when the Levites rallied to him and killed the idolaters.
b: After the golden calf, Moses stood at the gate of the camp and said, "Whoever is on the LORD's side, to me!" and the Levites gathered and killed three thousand (Exodus 32:26–28). Mattathias, a priest of Levi, gives the same call after an act of idolatry. Jesus' "Follow me" (Mark 1:17) uses the same verb pattern, but to a very different end.

a: They fled to the hills
p: Jesus tells those in Judea to 'flee to the mountains' when they see the abomination of desolation.
b: In Mark 13:14 and Matthew 24:15–16 Jesus says that when they see "the abomination of desolation" standing where it should not, "those in Judea must flee to the mountains." A Jewish hearer knew the pattern from this story: the abomination on the altar (1:54), then the faithful flee to the hills (2:28) and the desert (2:29). Hebrews 11:38 remembers those who wandered "in deserts and mountains, and in caves and holes in the ground."

a: many who sought what is right and just went down into the desert
p: The desert east of Jerusalem, with its caves, was the old refuge of David and later of the Qumran community.
b: The Judean desert falls steeply from the hills to the Dead Sea and is full of caves. David hid there from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14; 24:1–3), and in the following century a priestly community settled at Qumran "to prepare in the desert the way" (Isaiah 40:3, as quoted in their Community Rule). Josephus says the group of 2:29–38 were caught in caves near Jerusalem (Antiquities 12.272–275). "What is right and just" (dikaiosynē kai krima) is the pair Hebrew uses for faithful living under the law (Genesis 18:19; Isaiah 56:1).

a: We will not obey the king's word and profane the Sabbath day
p: These pious Jews held that the Sabbath command forbade even self-defense.
b: The law forbids work on the Sabbath and orders each person to "stay put in your own spot" (Exodus 16:29; 20:8–11). Many Jews of the time read this strictly. Jubilees, written in these same decades, lists "making war" among things that bring death on the Sabbath (Jubilees 50:12–13). 2 Maccabees 6:11 tells of people who gathered in caves to keep the Sabbath secretly and were burned to death, "because their piety kept them from defending themselves." To these Jews dying blameless was better than breaking the Sabbath.

a: Heaven and earth bear witness for us
p: Moses called heaven and earth to witness against Israel. Here the martyrs call them to witness for them.
b: "Today I call the heavens and the earth to testify against you" (Deuteronomy 30:19; compare Deuteronomy 31:28; Isaiah 1:2). The martyrs reverse it: creation itself will testify that they kept the covenant and were killed "without a trial" (akritōs). Their word for innocence, haplotēs ("integrity, singleness of heart"), is the word Mattathias uses of Daniel (2:60).
orig: ἐν τῇ ἁπλότητι ἡμῶν (en tē haplotēti hēmōn)

a: Whoever comes to make war on us on the Sabbath day, we will fight him face to face
p: Mattathias's group decided to defend themselves on the Sabbath. Jewish law later agreed; Christians debated it too.
b:
The ruling allows defense when attacked, not attack. Josephus says it held "to this day" (Antiquities 12.276–277) and tells how Pompey, in 63 BC, used it: since the Jews would fight back only if attacked, he built his siege mounds on the Sabbath unopposed (Antiquities 14.63–64). The Mishnah later gave the principle a wide form: danger to life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), and the Talmud cites "live by them" (Leviticus 18:5), not die by them (Babylonian Talmud Yoma 85b). A rabbinic saying on Exodus 31:13–14 runs, "The Sabbath is handed over to you, not you to the Sabbath" (Mekhilta), close to Jesus' "The Sabbath was made for man" (Mark 2:27).

Christians have read the verse beside Jesus' Sabbath healings (Luke 14:5; Matthew 12:11–12). Reformed confessions allow "works of necessity and mercy" on the Lord's Day (Westminster Confession 21.8). On whether Christians must keep the Sabbath at all, see the card at Exodus 20.

a: a company of Hasideans
p: Hebrew hasidim, 'the faithful, the devout': a group of law-keeping Jews who joined the revolt.
b:
The Greek Asidaioi renders Hebrew chasidim, "loyal ones," the word for God's faithful in the Psalms (Psalm 79:2, "your loyal ones"; Psalm 149:1). Here it seems to name an organized group, "a company" (synagōgē), strong and devoted to the law. They appear again at 7:12–17, where some of them trust the new high priest Alcimus and are killed, and 2 Maccabees 14:6 makes Judas their leader.

Who they were is debated. Older scholars made them the ancestors of both the Pharisees and the Essenes; many now think they were a looser movement of pious scribes, perhaps linked with the circles behind Daniel ("the wise," Daniel 11:33–35) and 1 Enoch's Animal Apocalypse (1 Enoch 90:6–9). Sinaiticus reads "a company of Jews" here (see the variant).

a: struck down sinners in their anger and lawless men in their rage
p: In 1 Maccabees 'sinners' and 'lawless men' are Jews who abandoned the law.
b: The book's words for the enemy inside Israel are "sinners" (hamartōloi), "lawless" (anomoi) and "renegades" (paranomoi). Gentiles are "the nations." Psalm 1's "sinners" and "wicked" are now a party. Paul, a Pharisee, uses the same language when he speaks of "Gentile sinners" and of himself as once "zealous" (Galatians 2:15; 1:14). The rest fled "to the nations," that is, to Gentile towns or to the Citadel.

a: they circumcised by force
p: The Greek en ischyi can mean 'by force' or 'with strength, boldly.' The KJV has 'valiantly.'
b: En ischyi is "in strength." Most modern readers take it as compulsion: the rebels circumcised boys whose parents had obeyed the king's ban (1:48, 60), so that the covenant sign was restored by force. The KJV's "valiantly" makes it an act of courage done in defiance of the decree. The book's own words in 1:58 ("they used their power," en ischyi, against Israel) suggest the first sense: the same power is now turned the other way. The later Hasmoneans forcibly circumcised Idumeans and Itureans (Josephus, Antiquities 13.257–258, 318).
orig: περιέτεμον τὰ παιδάρια τὰ ἀπερίτμητα (perietemon ta paidaria ta aperitmēta... en ischyi)

a: they did not let the sinner raise his horn
p: The horn is a picture of strength and pride, as in Psalm 75.
b: Literally "they did not give a horn to the sinner." In Hebrew poetry a raised horn is the pride and power of a wild ox (Psalm 75:4–5, "Do not raise your horn"; 1 Samuel 2:10). Daniel's visions turn the image into kings: horns on the beasts, the little horn that grows great (Daniel 7:8; 8:9). Mattathias's men kept the "horn" from rising again.
orig: καὶ οὐκ ἔδωκαν κέρας τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ (kai ouk edōkan keras tō hamartōlō)

a: As the time drew near for Mattathias to die, he said to his sons
p: Mattathias's testament follows the form of Jacob's blessing, Moses' farewell and David's charge to Solomon.
b: Dying fathers in Israel's story gather their sons and charge them: Jacob (Genesis 49), Moses (Deuteronomy 33), Joshua (Joshua 23–24), David (1 Kings 2:1–9). Mattathias's speech (2:49–68) has the same parts: the hour is grave; be zealous for the law; remember the ancestors; here is who will lead you. He ends with blessing and is "gathered to his ancestors" (2:69), as Jacob "was gathered to his people" (Genesis 49:33). The speech also does political work: it names Simon as counselor and "father" and Judas as general, which is the order the dynasty followed.

a: Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations
p: The list of faithful ancestors (2:52–60) is the model for Sirach 44–50 and Hebrews 11.
b:
Mattathias names eleven heroes in nine verses: Abraham, Joseph, Phinehas, Joshua, Caleb, David, Elijah, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Daniel. Each line pairs a virtue with a reward. Sirach 44–50, written about 180 BC, praises "famous men" in the same way, and 4 Maccabees 16:20–21 and 18:11–19 have shorter lists. Hebrews 11 is the Christian form: "by faith" Abraham, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, David, Samuel, and those who "shut the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire" (Hebrews 11:33–34).

The difference is telling. Mattathias's heroes are rewarded in this life: lordship, priesthood, land, a throne, rescue. Hebrews' heroes "died in faith, not having received what was promised" (Hebrews 11:13, 39).
r: Sirach 44:1–50:24; Hebrews 11:1–40; Hebrews 11:13; Hebrews 11:39; 4 Maccabees 16:20–21; 4 Maccabees 18:11–19

a: was he not found faithful in the test, and was it not reckoned to him as righteousness?
p: The line joins Genesis 15:6 to Genesis 22, as James does. Paul reads Genesis 15:6 apart from works.
b:
"Abram put his trust in the LORD, and he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6) is said in Genesis before the test of Genesis 22, where "God put Abraham to the test" (Genesis 22:1). Mattathias joins the two: Abraham was "found faithful (pistos) in the test (peirasmos), and it was reckoned to him." Sirach 44:20 and Jubilees 17–19 read Abraham the same way. James 2:21–23 also cites Genesis 15:6 as "fulfilled" when Abraham offered Isaac. Paul instead stresses that it was reckoned before circumcision and before any deed (Romans 4:3, 9–10; Galatians 3:6).

Here the passage agrees with Genesis and James in wording, and stands in tension with Paul's reading, depending on how Paul and James are reconciled. Some readers see faith and faithfulness joined here, as in James; others see Mattathias reading Genesis as many Jews of his day did, a reading Paul answered. On whether such deeds justify, see the Psalm 106 card on Phinehas and the Genesis 15 card.
r: Genesis 15:6; Genesis 22:1–18; James 2:21–23; Romans 4:3; Romans 4:9–10; Galatians 3:6; Sirach 44:20; Psalm 106:31

a: Joseph kept the commandment when he was hard pressed
p: Joseph refused Potiphar's wife: 'How could I do this great evil and sin against God?'
b: The "commandment" is the law against adultery, which Joseph kept when Potiphar's wife pressed him (Genesis 39:7–12): "So how could I do this great evil and sin against God?" (Genesis 39:9). The reward, "lord of Egypt," is Pharaoh's word, "See, I am putting you over all the land of Egypt" (Genesis 41:41; Psalm 105:21). Jubilees 39:6–7 also says Joseph remembered the law against adultery that Abraham taught.

a: received the covenant of a holy priesthood
p: Mattathias claims Phinehas as 'our father,' the ancestor of his priestly line.
b: Phinehas was Aaron's grandson, and every priest of the Second Temple counted him as an ancestor. God's promise was "a covenant of priesthood for all time" (Numbers 25:13). Alexandrinus says "holy priesthood"; Sinaiticus and Venetus, followed by the KJV, have "everlasting priesthood," matching Numbers (see the variant). Sirach 45:24 says the covenant gave Phinehas and his descendants the priesthood forever. For a family that would take the high priesthood, the line is a claim.

a: Joshua, because he carried out the word, became a judge in Israel
p: The Greek name Iēsous is Joshua; the KJV writes 'Jesus' here, as in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8.
b: Joshua's name in Greek is Iēsous, the same as Jesus. The KJV keeps "Jesus" here, as it does in Acts 7:45 and Hebrews 4:8, which modern versions render "Joshua." Calling Joshua a "judge" fits the book's picture of him as leader under the law; he "carried out the word" by bringing Israel into the land as Moses commanded (Joshua 1:7; 11:15).
orig: Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous)

a: Caleb bore witness before the assembly
p: Caleb and Joshua alone told the people the land was good and the LORD was with them.
b: When the scouts came back, Caleb and Joshua told "the whole community of Israelites" that "the land... is a good land, very, very good... the LORD is with us. Do not be afraid of them!" (Numbers 14:6–9). God promised, "my servant Caleb had a different spirit with him... So I will bring him into the land" (Numbers 14:24), and Joshua gave him Hebron (Joshua 14:6–14). The point for Mattathias's sons is plain: stand up to a frightened majority.

a: David, for his mercy, inherited the throne of a kingdom that lasts forever
p: The Greek eleos often renders Hebrew hesed, 'loyal love.' David spared Saul and was kind to Jonathan's son.
b: Eleos, "mercy," is the usual Septuagint word for hesed, "loyal love." David's mercy may mean his sparing of Saul (1 Samuel 24; 26) and his kindness to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1, 7), or the "faithful mercies of David" God promised (Isaiah 55:3). The reward is Nathan's promise, "Your throne will stand firm for all time" (2 Samuel 7:16). The line is striking in a book written for a dynasty that was not of David's line; on how the book treats the promise, see the note at 14:41.
orig: ἐν τῷ ἐλέει αὐτοῦ (en tō eleei autou)

a: was taken up as if into heaven
p: The small word hōs, 'as,' may hedge the claim that Elijah went into heaven itself.
b: 2 Kings 2:11 says "Elijah went up to the heavens in the windstorm," and the Septuagint there has hōs eis ton ouranon, "as it were into heaven," the same phrase as here. The "as" may reflect Hebrew idiom, or reverence: some Jewish readers held that no one ascends into God's own heaven (compare John 3:13, "nobody has gone up into heaven except the one who came down out of heaven"). Elijah's zeal is in 1 Kings 19:10: "I have burned with zeal for the LORD." Sirach 48:9 repeats "taken up in a whirlwind of fire."
orig: ἀνελήμφθη ὡς εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν (anelēmphthē hōs eis ton ouranon)

a: Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael trusted, and they were kept safe from the flame
p: Mattathias ends his list with the heroes of Daniel 3 and 6, the persecuted faithful of a foreign king's court.
b: The last two examples, the three young men in the furnace (Daniel 3) and Daniel in the lions' den (Daniel 6), are the only ones who suffered under a pagan king for refusing his worship, exactly the situation of 167 BC. Their Hebrew names are used, as in Daniel 1:6–7, not Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Hebrews 11:33–34 names the same rescues: those who "shut the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire." The phrase "abomination of desolation" (1:54) shows the writer also knew Daniel's visions.
r: Daniel 1:6–7; Daniel 3:16–28; Daniel 6:16–23; Hebrews 11:33–34; Prayer of Azariah

a: none who hope in him will grow weak
p: Mattathias does not say 'God' or 'the Lord.' The book avoids naming God throughout.
b: In Swete's Greek of 1 Maccabees, the word "God" (theos) never appears in chapters 1–4, and "Lord" (kyrios) appears only of Joseph as "lord of Egypt" (2:53); Sinaiticus and Venetus add "God" in a few places (3:18), and the KJV and Vulgate add it often (3:22; 3:53; 4:10; 4:24; 4:55). God is "him" (2:61; 3:22), "Heaven" (3:18–19, 50, 60; 4:10, 24, 40, 55), or "you" in prayer (3:50–53; 4:30–33). The habit matches later Jewish reverence for the divine name (Daniel 4:26, "Heaven rules"; Matthew's "kingdom of heaven"). The thought of the line is that of Psalm 22:5 and Isaiah 40:31.
orig: πάντες οἱ ἐλπίζοντες ἐπ᾽ αὐτὸν οὐκ ἀσθενήσουσιν (pantes hoi elpizontes ep' auton ouk asthenēsousin)

a: his glory will go to dung and worms
p: The sinful man is Antiochus. Both 2 Maccabees and Acts tell of proud kings eaten by worms.
b: "His breath leaves, he goes back to his ground; that same day his schemes are gone" (Psalm 146:4), and 2:63 nearly quotes it. Isaiah mocks the king of Babylon: "Under you, maggots make your mattress; worms are your bedcovers" (Isaiah 14:11), and Job 20:7 says the wicked will perish "like his own dung." 2 Maccabees 9:9 says Antiochus died with worms swarming from his body; Acts 12:23 says the same of Herod Agrippa, who took divine honors. 1 Maccabees 6:8–16 tells Antiochus's death more soberly.

a: He will be a father to you
p: Mattathias names Simon as the family's 'father' and Judas as its general, the order history followed.
b: Simon was the last of the brothers to lead and the one who founded the dynasty: he took the Citadel (13:49–52), won freedom from tribute (13:41–42) and was made high priest, general and leader "forever" by the people (14:41–47). Mattathias's testament reads like an endorsement of that outcome, which is one reason many scholars think the book was written under Simon's son, John Hyrcanus (died 104 BC), or soon after (see 16:23–24).

a: you will wage the war of the peoples
p: An unclear phrase. It may mean the war against the Gentile peoples, or a war on behalf of the people.
b: Alexandrinus has "you will fight (polemēsete) the war of peoples"; Sinaiticus and Venetus have "he will fight," with Judas as subject, which the KJV follows ("fight the battle of the people"). Laōn, "of peoples," is plural, so most take it as war against the nations around Israel, the wars of chapter 5. Others think it renders a Hebrew phrase for Israel's own wars (compare "Israel's war," 3:2).
orig: καὶ πολεμήσετε πόλεμον λαῶν (kai polemēsete polemon laōn)

a: take vengeance for your people
p: Mattathias's charge to avenge sounds harsh, but it echoes the Song of Moses, where God avenges his servants.
b: The Song of Moses ends, "He will avenge his sons' blood and turn vengeance back on his foes" (Deuteronomy 32:43), and Psalm 79:10, a lament for the defiled Temple, asks for "the vengeance for your servants' blood that was spilled." Mattathias puts that vengeance in his sons' hands. Paul will tell Christians the reverse: "never avenge yourselves... vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord" (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35). Readers of the book have to weigh both.

a: He died in the year 146
p: The year 146 is 166 BC. Mattathias led the revolt for about a year.
b: Mattathias's revolt began after the decree of 167 BC and he died in 166 BC, so his own leadership was short. Josephus says he had led for one year (Antiquities 12.285). Mourning by all Israel is told of great leaders: "All Israel came together to mourn" Samuel (1 Samuel 25:1), and later of Judas (9:20) and Jonathan (13:26).

a: He made his people's glory wide
p: 3:3–9 is a poem in praise of Judas, probably once in Hebrew, like the songs for Saul and David.
b: The book pauses its story for a hymn of seven verses in parallel lines. Women once sang "Saul has struck his thousands, David his tens of thousands" (1 Samuel 18:7), and David lamented Saul and Jonathan as stronger than lions (2 Samuel 1:23). Sirach praises Simon the high priest in a similar hymn (Sirach 50:1–21). Some scholars think the poem was composed after Judas's death, as an epitaph; it reads like the praise of a dead hero ("his memory will be a blessing forever," 3:7).

a: He dressed in a breastplate like a giant
p: The Greek gigas is the Septuagint word for the mighty warriors of old, and for the sun running its course.
b: In the Septuagint gigas renders Hebrew gibbor, "mighty man, warrior": Nimrod is "a giant hunter" (Genesis 10:8–9 LXX), and in the Greek of Psalm 19:5 (numbered 18:6 there) the sun goes out "like a giant" to run its course. The word here means a champion, not a monster. The irony is that David beat the giant who wore the breastplate (1 Samuel 17:5, 38).
orig: ἐνεδύσατο θώρακα ὡς γίγας (enedysato thōraka hōs gigas)

a: like a young lion that roars on the hunt
p: Jacob called Judah 'a lion's cub.' The poem gives Judas, named for Judah, the same image.
b: Jacob's blessing says, "Judah is a lion's cub; you have come up from the prey, my son" (Genesis 49:9), and Balaam sees Israel rise "like a lion" that does not lie down until it eats its prey (Numbers 23:24). Judas bears the patriarch's name, and the poem claims Judah's blessing for him. Revelation applies the same blessing to Christ, "the Lion from the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5). A reader who knows both can see how one image served two very different hopes.

a: he set fire to those who troubled his people
p: The Greek ephlogisen means 'he set ablaze.' 2 Maccabees tells of Judas burning those who had burned others.
b: Phlogizō is "to set on fire." It may be a figure for destroying, or literal: 2 Maccabees 8:33 says that Judas's men burned those who had set fire to the Temple gates, and 1 Maccabees 5:5, 44 tells of towns and a temple burned. The Hebrew original may have had a word like bi'er, "burn out, sweep away," used in Deuteronomy's formula "sweep the evil out" (Deuteronomy 13:5; 17:7).
orig: καὶ τοὺς ταράσσοντας τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ἐφλόγισεν (kai tous tarassontas ton laon autou ephlogisen)

a: all who did lawless deeds
p: A stock phrase of the Greek Psalms, used by Jesus in Matthew 7:23.
b: Hoi ergatai tēs anomias, "the workers of lawlessness," is close to the Septuagint's phrase hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian for evildoers in the Psalms (Psalm 6:8, "every one of you who does wrong"; Psalm 5:5; 14:4). Jesus uses that phrase of those he will send away: "Leave me, you who practice lawlessness!" (Matthew 7:23, quoting Psalm 6:8).
orig: πάντες οἱ ἐργάται τῆς ἀνομίας (pantes hoi ergatai tēs anomias)

a: and he turned anger away from Israel
p: Judas does for Israel what Phinehas did at Peor: he turns God's anger away.
b: The verse answers 1:64 ("a very great wrath fell on Israel") with the words God used of Phinehas: he "has turned my rage back from the Israelites" (Numbers 25:11). In the book's view, the anger was God's response to apostasy, and wiping out the apostates ends it. 2 Maccabees 8:5 says the same in plainer words: once Judas gathered his army, "the wrath of the Lord had turned to mercy."

a: Apollonius gathered the nations, with a large force from Samaria
p: Probably the commander of 1:29 (the 'Mysarch' of 2 Maccabees 5:24), and governor of the district of Samaria.
b: Josephus calls this Apollonius the governor (stratēgos) of Samaria (Antiquities 12.287), and many identify him with the Apollonius who sacked Jerusalem in 167 BC (1:29; 2 Maccabees 5:24). Samaria was a separate district from Judea under the Seleucids, and its troops would include both Greek settlers and local people. The battle is undated and its place unnamed; Josephus adds nothing more.

a: Judas took the sword of Apollonius
p: Like David with Goliath's sword, Judas fights with the sword of the man he killed.
b: David killed Goliath with the Philistine's own sword and later took it from the priests at Nob, saying, "Nothing compares to it. Give it to me" (1 Samuel 21:9; see 1 Samuel 17:51). The book often frames Judas as a new David: the prayer at Beth-zur names David and Goliath (4:30), and the Philistines are the enemy again (3:24, 41; 4:22).

a: a company of the faithful
p: The Greek ekklēsia, 'assembly,' is the Septuagint word for Israel gathered before God, later the word for 'church.'
b: Ekklēsia renders Hebrew qahal, the assembly of Israel (Deuteronomy 9:10; 31:30). 1 Maccabees uses it for Israel gathered for war or decision (3:13; 4:59; 5:16; 14:19). The New Testament takes it over for the community of Christ's followers, "the church." The Douay in 4:59 renders it "all the church of Israel."
orig: ἐκκλησίαν πιστῶν (ekklēsian pistōn)

a: the ascent of Beth-horon
p: The main road from the coast up to Jerusalem, where Joshua routed the Amorites.
b: The road from the coastal plain climbs to the Jerusalem plateau along a ridge between Lower and Upper Beth-horon. It is narrow and steep, ideal for an ambush from above. Joshua chased the Amorite kings "up the Beth-horon pass" and down its slope (Joshua 10:10–11); the Philistines used it (1 Samuel 13:18); Solomon fortified Upper and Lower Beth-horon (2 Chronicles 8:5); Judas would win here again against Nicanor (7:39–43), and in AD 66 Jewish rebels routed a Roman legion in the same pass (Josephus, War 2.546–550). Alexandrinus misspells the name here (see the variant).

a: To Heaven it makes no difference whether it saves by many or by few
p: Judas quotes Jonathan's faith in 1 Samuel 14: 'He can save with many or with few.'
b: Jonathan told his armor-bearer, "The LORD is not held back. He can save with many or with few" (1 Samuel 14:6), and Asa prayed, "for you there is no difference in helping, whether the side is great or has no strength" (2 Chronicles 14:11). Gideon's army was cut to three hundred so that Israel would not say, "My own hand rescued me" (Judges 7:2). Judas says the same, but with "Heaven" where the old texts have "the LORD"; see the next note.

a: Heaven
p: Judas says 'Heaven' rather than 'God.' Jews of this time often used the word to avoid naming God.
b:
The Greek is tou ouranou, "of heaven." Sinaiticus and Venetus, with the KJV and Vulgate, read "the God of heaven" (see the variant), but Alexandrinus's shorter text fits the whole book, which never uses the word God (see the note at 2:61). The Plain capitalizes "Heaven" where it stands for God.

The usage is old: Daniel says "Heaven rules" (Daniel 4:26), and the Mishnah speaks of "the fear of Heaven" and "the name of Heaven" (Mishnah Avot 1:3; 4:4). In the New Testament the prodigal son says "I have sinned against heaven" (Luke 15:18, 21), and Matthew's "kingdom of heaven" is Mark's and Luke's "kingdom of God" (Matthew 4:17; Mark 1:15).
orig: ἐναντίον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ (enantion tou ouranou), 'before Heaven'
r: Daniel 4:26; Luke 15:18; Luke 15:21; Matthew 4:17; Mark 1:15; Mishnah Avot 1:3

a: Strength comes from Heaven
t: Not by the size of an army
p: David told Goliath 'the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear.' Psalm 33 says the same of armies.
b: "Everyone gathered here will learn that the LORD saves, and not by sword and spear. The battle belongs to the LORD" (1 Samuel 17:47). "A king does not win safety by having a big army" (Psalm 33:16). Zechariah 4:6 has "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit." 1 Maccabees keeps this faith in every battle of Judas, even while it carefully records the numbers, the tactics and the weapons.

a: We, though, are fighting for our lives and our laws
t: A war for life and law
p: Judas frames the war as defense of life and religion, the classic case of a just war.
b: The aim is limited: the rebels fight "for our lives and our laws" (also 2:40; 13:3), against an army coming "to destroy us and our wives and our children, and to plunder us" (3:20). Ambrose praised the Maccabees' courage in defending the law (On the Duties of the Clergy 1.40–41), and Aquinas cited Mattathias's decision of 2:41 when he asked whether war may be waged on holy days (Summa Theologiae II-II q.40 a.4). Others note that the same book records conquests and forced conversions (2:46; 5:68) that go beyond defense. On Christians and war, see the card at Deuteronomy 20.

a: the land of the Philistines
p: The Greek allophyloi, 'foreigners,' is the Septuagint's word for the Philistines. Here it means the coastal cities.
b: The Philistine people had long since disappeared, but the Septuagint uses allophyloi, "people of another tribe," for them, and 1 Maccabees calls the Greek cities of the coast (Azotus, Gaza, Ascalon) by the old name. The Plain gives "Philistines" where it means that land (3:24, 41; 4:22; 4:30) and "foreigners" elsewhere (4:12, 26). The choice keeps the book's echo of Saul's and David's wars.
orig: εἰς γῆν Φυλιστιείμ (eis gēn Phylistieim)

a: by doing away with the laws that had stood from the earliest days
p: The book blames Antiochus's money troubles on his own war against Judea's laws.
b: Antiochus III had confirmed the Jews' right to live by their ancestral laws when he took Judea in about 200 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 12.138–144). His son undid it. The Seleucid treasury was also burdened by the indemnity owed to Rome after Magnesia, so a revolt that cut tax income hurt. Daniel says the king of the north will "scatter plunder, spoil and goods" among his followers (Daniel 11:24), and Polybius tells of Antiochus's lavish gifts and games at Daphne in 166 BC (Histories 30.25–26), the "open hand" of 3:30.

a: he decided to go to Persia
p: In 165 BC Antiochus marched east to raise money and restore control. He died there late in 164 BC.
b: "Persia" here means the eastern provinces in general ("the upper provinces," 3:37). The king took half the army across the Euphrates in 165 BC; he died at Tabae in Persis in late 164 BC, after a failed attempt to rob a temple (6:1–16; 2 Maccabees 9; Polybius, Histories 31.9). A Babylonian king list records that the news of his death was heard in Babylon in year 148, probably in Kislev, the month of the rededication (4:52); the month name is restored. Daniel 11:44 has the king alarmed by "reports from the east and the north."

a: to bring up his son Antiochus until he came back
p: The son became Antiochus V Eupator at about nine years old, with Lysias as regent.
b: Antiochus V was born about 173 BC. After his father's death Lysias ruled in his name (6:17), until Demetrius I, the son of Seleucus IV and the hostage in Rome, escaped, took the throne and had both killed in 162 BC (7:1–4). The rival claims of the two branches of the family will shape everything in the rest of the book.

a: to settle foreigners in all their territory
p: The order would have done to Judea what Assyria did to Samaria.
b: When Assyria took Samaria, it brought "people from Babylon, from Cuthah, from Avva, from Hamath and Sepharvaim" to live in Israel's towns (2 Kings 17:24). Antiochus's order to "divide their land" by lot (the Greek kataklēronomēsai is the word used for Joshua's dividing of Canaan, Joshua 14:1) is a conquest in reverse. Daniel 11:39 says the king "will divide the land for a price."

a: Ptolemy son of Dorymenes, Nicanor and Gorgias
p: 2 Maccabees adds details: Ptolemy was governor of Coele-Syria, and Nicanor would sell the Jews as slaves.
b: 2 Maccabees 8:8–10 says Ptolemy, governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, sent Nicanor son of Patroclus, "one of the king's First Friends," with Gorgias, a general experienced in war. It gives the army as 20,000 (2 Maccabees 8:9), against 47,000 here (3:39). This Nicanor may not be the Nicanor of chapter 7, whose defeat is Nicanor's Day (7:26–50). Ptolemy son of Dorymenes is also the man who, according to 2 Maccabees 4:45–50, was bribed to free Menelaus.

a: forty thousand men and seven thousand horsemen
p: Historians think the book's numbers for the enemy are inflated. Venetus gives fifty thousand.
b: Bar-Kochva, who studied Seleucid army sizes in detail, judged that the king could not have sent 47,000 men to Judea while he took half the army east, and that 2 Maccabees' 20,000 is nearer the truth. Inflated numbers for the enemy were common in ancient war writing, and they serve the book's theme that strength comes from Heaven (3:19). Codex Venetus has "fifty thousand" for forty (Swete's apparatus).

a: near Emmaus in the lowland
p: Emmaus-Nicopolis, at the edge of the hills about 19 miles west of Jerusalem. Is it Luke's Emmaus?
b: This Emmaus is the town later called Nicopolis (modern 'Imwas, near Latrun), where the Ayalon valley meets the hills. Luke's Emmaus is "sixty stadia" (about 7 miles) from Jerusalem (Luke 24:13); a few manuscripts, including Sinaiticus, read 160 stadia, which would fit this Emmaus, and Eusebius and Jerome identified the two. Most scholars think Luke's Emmaus was a nearer village, but the question is still debated.

a: and servants
p: The Greek paidas means 'servants.' Many scholars think the original said 'fetters,' to chain the slaves.
b: The merchants bring money and paidas, "servants, slaves," to buy Israelites as slaves. The KJV and the Vulgate (pueros) have "servants." Many modern scholars and some versions read pedas, "fetters," spelled differently but pronounced alike in the Greek of the time, which fits the scene better. Josephus's retelling has the merchants bring bonds for the captives (Antiquities 12.299), and Goldstein reports that the Syriac version supports it. The Plain keeps the Greek of all three codices. 2 Maccabees 8:10–11 says Nicanor had promised to sell the captives at ninety slaves for a talent.
orig: καὶ παῖδας (kai paidas)

a: Jerusalem lay empty like a desert
p: The poem draws on Lamentations and on Jeremiah's threat to silence the voices of joy.
b: "The roads to Zion are in mourning, because no one comes to the feasts" (Lamentations 1:4). Jeremiah had warned that God would silence "the sound of joy and the sound of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride" (Jeremiah 7:34; 16:9), and Isaiah 24:8 that "the joy of the lyre is silent." The flute and harp (aulos and kinyra, the Hebrew kinnor) were the instruments of the Temple's song, which would sound again at the rededication (4:54).

a: came to Mizpah, opposite Jerusalem
p: Samuel gathered Israel at Mizpah to fast and pray before a Philistine attack. Judas does the same.
b: "Bring all Israel together at Mizpah, and I will pray for you to the LORD." There "they went without food that day," and the LORD thundered against the Philistines (1 Samuel 7:5–10). Mizpah (Greek Massēpha), usually identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, about 8 miles north of Jerusalem, was also where Israel gathered against Benjamin (Judges 20:1) and where Saul was chosen king (1 Samuel 10:17). With the Temple in enemy hands, the people go to the old place of prayer.

a: That day they fasted
p: Sackcloth, ashes and torn clothes: the signs of national repentance from Samuel to Nehemiah.
b: Israel fasted before battle at Bethel (Judges 20:26) and at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:6); Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast when enemies came (2 Chronicles 20:3); Ezra fasted before the journey (Ezra 8:21–23), and Nehemiah's people came together "fasting and dressed in sackcloth, with soil on them" (Nehemiah 9:1). Judith's people do the same before Holofernes (Judith 4:9–15).
r: Judges 20:26; 1 Samuel 7:6; 2 Chronicles 20:3; Ezra 8:21–23; Nehemiah 9:1; Judith 4:9–15

a: to search it on matters the nations used to ask of the images of their idols
p: Either Israel looked in the law for the guidance pagans sought from idols, or the pagans had painted idols on the scrolls.
b:
The Greek, "they spread out the scroll of the law, concerning which the nations searched out the likenesses of their idols," has puzzled readers since antiquity. Three readings are proposed:

(1) The Plain's: the people consulted the law, as pagans consulted their gods' images before battle; with no prophet and no priest's Urim, they sought a sign in the law (compare Numbers 27:21; 1 Samuel 14:37). (2) The KJV's "wherein the heathen had sought to paint the likeness of their images" and the Douay's "in which the Gentiles searched for the likeness of their idols": the persecutors had defaced the scrolls or searched them for Greek gods. (3) Goldstein and others suspect a damaged Hebrew original. The verse also shows that some scrolls survived the burning of 1:56.
orig: περὶ ὧν ἐξηρεύνων τὰ ἔθνη τὰ ὁμοιώματα τῶν εἰδώλων αὐτῶν (peri hōn exēreunōn ta ethnē ta homoiōmata tōn eidōlōn autōn)

a: the Nazirites who had completed their days
p: Priests' robes, firstfruits, tithes and Nazirite vows all needed the Temple. The people bring them as a protest.
b: Firstfruits and tithes belonged at the sanctuary (Deuteronomy 26:1–4; Numbers 18:21–26). A Nazirite whose vow was finished had to bring offerings at the sanctuary and shave his head there (Numbers 6:13–20, "when his time of being set apart is over"). With the Temple defiled, none of this could be done. The people lay it all before Heaven and ask, "What are we to do with these?" (3:50). Paul later paid for Nazirite offerings at the Temple (Acts 21:23–26).
r: Numbers 6:13–20; Deuteronomy 26:1–4; Numbers 18:21–26; Acts 21:23–26; Mishnah Nazir 5:4

a: Your holy place is trampled and profaned
p: The image of the Temple trampled by the nations runs from Isaiah to Daniel, Luke and Revelation.
b: "Our foes have trampled your sanctuary" (Isaiah 63:18); Daniel's vision asks "how long" the sanctuary and host will be "trampled" (Daniel 8:13). Jesus says Jerusalem "will be trampled by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled" (Luke 21:24), and Revelation 11:2 gives the outer court to the nations "to trample" for forty-two months. 1 Maccabees uses the word at 3:45, 51 and 4:60.

a: They sounded the trumpets
p: The law says that when Israel blows the trumpets for battle, God will remember them.
b: "When you go out to battle in your own land against an enemy who is attacking you, sound the battle blast on the trumpets. Then the LORD your God will remember you, and you will be rescued from your enemies" (Numbers 10:9). The priests blew trumpets in Abijah's battle (2 Chronicles 13:12–14). The trumpets at Mizpah are part of the prayer, and they sound again at Emmaus (4:13) and in the Temple (4:40).

a: commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens
p: Judas organizes Israel as Moses did in the wilderness.
b: Jethro advised Moses to "set them over the people as captains of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties and of tens" (Exodus 18:21; Deuteronomy 1:15). The Qumran War Scroll uses the same units for the final war of the Sons of Light (1QM 4). Judas's army is presented as Israel of the wilderness, camped and ready for holy war.

a: as the law says
p: Judas sends home the men Deuteronomy 20 releases from battle, though he can hardly spare them.
b: The officials are to send home anyone who has built a new house, planted a vineyard, or been "promised a woman in marriage," and anyone "afraid and fainthearted" (Deuteronomy 20:5–8). Gideon did the same (Judges 7:3). Keeping the rule when outnumbered is a statement of faith: the battle is Heaven's (3:19). The Mishnah later limited these exemptions to wars of choice, not commanded wars (Mishnah Sotah 8:7).

a: Arm yourselves and be brave men
p: The call echoes the Philistines' cry at Aphek and Joab's before battle.
b: The Philistines urged each other, "Act like men and fight!" (1 Samuel 4:9), and Joab said, "Be strong. Let's stand firm and be strong for the sake of our people and our God's cities. The LORD will do whatever he sees is good" (2 Samuel 10:12). Judas's speech has both halves: courage (3:58–59) and surrender to God's will (3:60). Paul writes, "Stand firm in the faith, be men, be strong" (1 Corinthians 16:13).

a: But whatever the will in Heaven is, so he will do
p: Judas's last words before battle sound like the Lord's Prayer: God's will as it is in heaven.
b: Joab ended his battle speech, "The LORD will do whatever he sees is good" (2 Samuel 10:12), and Eli said, "He is the LORD. Let him do whatever looks good to him" (1 Samuel 3:18). Judas speaks of "the will in Heaven," which a Christian reader hears in "May your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth" (Matthew 6:10) and in Jesus' prayer in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:39). The KJV adds "of God" here, a word the Greek does not have.

a: this force set out by night
p: Gorgias tried a surprise attack by night. Judas left his camp empty and struck the main camp instead.
b: Gorgias took about an eighth of the army to catch the rebels in their camp at dawn, guided by men from the Citadel who knew the hills (4:2). Judas learned of it, left his camp, and attacked the enemy's base while its strength was away (4:3–4). Bar-Kochva reconstructs the battle in detail and judges the account sound: a light force using the hills and the night against a divided professional army. 2 Maccabees 8:23–29 tells the battle differently, as a straight fight against Nicanor ending at the Sabbath.

a: They lacked the shields and swords they would have wanted
p: Like Israel in Saul's day, when 'neither sword nor spear was found' among the people.
b: When the Philistines held the land, "not one of the people who followed Saul and Jonathan held a sword or a spear" (1 Samuel 13:22). Judas's three thousand were in the same state: the book stresses the gap between them and the enemy's breastplates and cavalry (4:7), so that the victory is Heaven's.

a: Remember how our ancestors were saved at the Red Sea
p: Judas recalls the Exodus: Pharaoh's army pursued, and God saved Israel.
b: "Egypt chased after them, every horse of Pharaoh's chariots, his horsemen and his army" (Exodus 14:9), and Moses told the people, "Do not be afraid. Take your stand, and see how the LORD will save you today" (Exodus 14:13). Judas uses the same two words: "Do not be afraid" (4:8) and "remember." The Exodus is the pattern for every later rescue in Israel's story.

a: Perhaps he will want us still
p: Judas does not presume on God. The 'perhaps' of prayer runs through the prophets.
b: The Greek ei thelēsei hēmas, "if he will want us," has the cautious hope of Jonathan ("Maybe the LORD will act for us," 1 Samuel 14:6) and of Joel and Jonah's king ("Who knows? He may turn and relent," Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9). The KJV adds "the Lord will have mercy upon us," which the Greek here lacks (see the variant).
orig: εἰ θελήσει ἡμᾶς (ei thelēsei hēmas)

a: remember the covenant with our ancestors
p: 'God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob' began the Exodus. Judas asks for the same.
b: When Israel cried out in Egypt, "God heard their groans. God remembered his covenant, the one with Abraham, with Isaac and with Jacob" (Exodus 2:24). Leviticus 26:42–45 promises that even in exile God will remember the covenant with the ancestors. Mattathias's last words had told his sons to give their lives "for the covenant of our ancestors" (2:50).

a: Then every nation will know that Israel has someone who redeems and rescues it
p: David said the same to Goliath: the battle will show the world that Israel has a God.
b: "This very day the LORD will hand you over to me ... Then all the earth will know there is a God who belongs to Israel" (1 Samuel 17:46). Hezekiah prayed that "every kingdom on earth will know that you, LORD, are God, and only you" (2 Kings 19:19). The Greek ho lytroumenos, "the one who redeems," is the word of the Exodus (Exodus 6:6) and of Isaiah's "redeemer" (Isaiah 41:14).
orig: ὅτι ἔστιν ὁ λυτρούμενος καὶ σώζων τὸν Ἰσραήλ (hoti estin ho lytroumenos kai sōzōn ton Israēl)

a: Gazara
p: Gezer, Ashdod and Yavneh: the pursuit ran west and south to the edge of the coastal plain.
b: Gazara is Old Testament Gezer, guarding the road from the coast to Jerusalem (1 Kings 9:15–17); Simon would later take it and make it a Jewish city (13:43–48). Azotus is Ashdod, the Philistine city of the ark story (1 Samuel 5:1), and Jamnia is Yavneh, where the rabbis would gather after AD 70. Fleeing west, the enemy ran for the Greek cities of the coast.

a: Don't crave the plunder
p: Achan's sin at Jericho and Saul's at Amalek were taking plunder too soon. Judas holds his men back.
b: Plunder was lawful in war (Deuteronomy 20:14), but greed could ruin a battle: Achan's taking from Jericho brought defeat at Ai (Joshua 7), and Saul was rebuked because he chose to "swoop down on the spoil" (1 Samuel 15:19).
