Judas makes his men wait until the second enemy force is gone (4:18). 2 Maccabees 8:27–28 adds that they gave a share of the plunder to the widows, orphans and those who had been tortured.

a: blue and purple cloth, purple from the sea
p: The costly dyes came from sea snails. Blue and purple were the colors of the Tabernacle and of kings.
b: The Greek hyakinthos and porphyra are the Septuagint's words for the blue and purple yarn of the Tabernacle (Exodus 25:4). Alexandrinus reads "purple and sea," short for porphyra thalassia, "sea purple," which names the dye from the murex snail, worked at Tyre and Sidon and worth more than its weight in silver. The plunder shows the wealth of the army, and perhaps of the slave dealers who came with it (3:41).
orig: ὑάκινθον καὶ πορφύραν καὶ θαλασσίαν (hyakinthon kai porphyran kai thalassian)

a: For his loyal love is good forever
p: The refrain of Psalms 118 and 136, sung by the Levites before Jehoshaphat's army.
b: "Give thanks to the LORD, for he is good, for his loyal love is forever" (Psalm 136:1; also Psalm 118:1). It was sung when the ark entered the Temple (2 Chronicles 5:13), at the foundation of the second Temple (Ezra 3:11), and by singers going out ahead of the army (2 Chronicles 20:21). Alexandrinus has the short form, "for good forever is his mercy"; Sinaiticus and Venetus give the fuller form, which the KJV follows (see the variant).
orig: Ὅτι καλὸν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα τὸ ἔλεος αὐτοῦ (hoti kalon eis ton aiōna to eleos autou)

a: The next year
t: Beth-zur: before or after the cleansing?
p: 1 Maccabees puts Lysias's first campaign before the rededication; 2 Maccabees after it.
b: Here Lysias attacks in the year after Emmaus (165/164 BC) and is beaten at Beth-zur, opening the way to the Temple. 2 Maccabees 11:1–15 tells the campaign after the rededication and the death of Antiochus IV, and ends it with a negotiated peace and letters, one dated to 148 SE (2 Maccabees 11:16–38). Many historians think 1 Maccabees' order is right and its account simplified: the letters suggest Lysias negotiated rather than simply fled (4:35). The two accounts conflict on order and outcome.

a: camped at Beth-zur
p: A hill fortress on the road from Hebron to Jerusalem, the border between Judea and Idumea.
b: Beth-zur (Khirbet et-Tubeiqa, about 4 miles north of Hebron) was one of Rehoboam's fortified towns (2 Chronicles 11:7). By this time the land to the south, including Hebron, was Idumean, so Lysias came up from the south rather than through the hostile hills to the west. Judas fortified it as a fortress "facing Idumea" (4:61); Lysias took it later (6:31, 49–50).

a: You broke the mighty man's charge by the hand of your servant David
p: Judas recalls two victories by the few: David's over Goliath and Jonathan's raid on the Philistines.
b: The prayer names David's fight with Goliath (1 Samuel 17) and Jonathan's raid with his armor-bearer on the Philistine post at Michmash (1 Samuel 14:1–23). Both stories begin with a man who trusts God against a stronger foe, and both lead to Israel's rout of the Philistines. They are the book's model for Judas, already echoed at 3:12 and 3:18.

a: Savior of Israel
p: A title of God in Isaiah and Jeremiah. Seleucid kings also called themselves 'Savior.'
b: "For I am the LORD, your God, the Holy One of Israel, the one who saves you" (Isaiah 43:3); "Hope of Israel, its Savior in time of trouble" (Jeremiah 14:8). Sōtēr was also a royal title: Antiochus I and Demetrius I bore the name Soter. In the New Testament the title passes to Jesus (Luke 2:11; Acts 13:23).
orig: ὁ σωτὴρ Ἰσραήλ (ho sōtēr Israēl)

a: Let their bold strength melt away
p: The prayer asks God to do to the enemy what Canaan's dread did before Joshua.
b: Rahab told the spies, "When we heard it, our hearts melted. Because of you no one has any spirit left" (Joshua 2:11; also Joshua 5:1). God promised to send his terror ahead of Israel (Exodus 23:27) and to give the enemy a fearful heart (Leviticus 26:36). Judas prays that the terror once on Israel may fall on the nations.

a: how ready they were either to live or to die nobly
t: To live or to die nobly
p: The ideal of a noble death, honored by Greeks and Jews alike, is the spirit of the martyr stories.
b: The phrase zēn ē tethnēkenai gennaiōs, "to live or to die nobly," is Greek in style; Greek writers praised soldiers ready for a fine death. 2 Maccabees 6:28 has the scribe Eleazar leave the young an example: "to meet a good death eagerly and bravely for the solemn and holy laws," where "bravely" is the same Greek word, gennaiōs. Paul's "to live is Christ and to die is gain" (Philippians 1:21) belongs to the same world of thought. On the martyrs, see 2:37 and the topic page.
orig: ἢ ζῇν ἢ τεθνηκέναι γενναίως (ē zēn ē tethnēkenai gennaiōs)

a: Now let us go up and make the holy place clean, and dedicate it again
p: The goal of the whole war so far: Judas's first act after victory is to restore the Temple's worship.
b: Hezekiah had cleansed the Temple after his father's idolatry, in sixteen days (2 Chronicles 29:15–19), and Josiah removed the idols of Manasseh (2 Kings 23:4–12). Daniel's vision had promised that after 2,300 evenings and mornings "the sanctuary will be made right" (Daniel 8:14). The Greek katharisai and enkainisai, "cleanse" and "renew," give the feast its Greek name, enkainia (John 10:22).
orig: καθαρίσαι τὰ ἅγια καὶ ἐνκαινίσαι (katharisai ta hagia kai enkainisai)

a: Plants had grown up in the courtyards as in a forest or on a hillside
p: The ruined Temple looks like the desolation the prophets foretold for Zion.
b: Micah warned that "Zion will be plowed like a field ... and the Temple mount will become a wooded hill" (Micah 3:12, quoted in Jeremiah 26:18), and Lamentations mourns "Mount Zion, which lies desolate; jackals prowl over it" (Lamentations 5:18). In three years of neglect, the courts have grown wild.

a: He picked priests who were without blemish and who loved the law
p: Judas chose priests not tainted by the Hellenizers. The law required priests without physical defects.
b: Leviticus 21:17–23 bars any priest with a physical defect from offering at the altar; "without blemish" may mean that, but "who loved the law" points to loyalty: many priests had joined the Greek games (2 Maccabees 4:14–15). The high priest Menelaus was still in office under the king; the book does not name him, or say who led the new worship. Josephus later says Judas himself was high priest (Antiquities 12.414), which 1 Maccabees does not claim.

a: took the stones that had been defiled out to an unclean place
p: The law of a house with mold: defiled stones are taken out to an unclean place outside the city.
b: If a house has a spreading mold, the priest is to order the infected stones torn out and "thrown into an unclean place outside the city" (Leviticus 14:40, 45). Judas's men treat the stones of the pagan altar the same way. The Mishnah records that the Hasmoneans hid away the stones "the kings of Greece had defiled" (Mishnah Middot 1:6).

a: until a prophet should come to give a ruling about them
p: No one could rule on the stones of a holy altar defiled by pagans. The question waits for a prophet.
b:
The altar of burnt offering was holy (Exodus 29:37), but the nations had defiled it, so the priests could neither use it nor throw it away. They store its stones "until a prophet should come." The book says the same of Simon's high priesthood, "until a faithful prophet arises" (14:41), and speaks of the day "a prophet was last seen among them" (9:27). Psalm 74:9, which many date to this time or the Babylonian ruin, says, "There is no prophet now." The hope may draw on Deuteronomy 18:18, the prophet like Moses, or on Malachi 4:5, the coming of Elijah.

Jewish tradition holds that prophecy ceased after Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi (Tosefta Sotah 13:3), and Josephus that the exact succession of prophets ended under Artaxerxes (Against Apion 1.41). Protestant and Catholic writers draw opposite conclusions from such verses about the canon; see the card on the book page.
orig: μέχρι τοῦ παραγενηθῆναι προφήτην (mechri tou paragenēthēnai prophētēn)

a: They took whole stones, as the law says
p: The law said an altar of stone must be built of uncut stones, untouched by iron.
b: "If you make me an altar of stones, do not build it of cut stone. If you have swung your blade over it, you have made it unholy" (Exodus 20:25). Moses commanded the altar on Mount Ebal to be built of "whole, uncut stones" (Deuteronomy 27:6; Joshua 8:31). The Mishnah explains that iron, made to shorten life, may not touch the altar, made to lengthen it (Mishnah Middot 3:4).

a: he consecrated the courts
p: Alexandrinus says 'he consecrated,' singular, where the other verbs are plural. 'He' is presumably Judas.
b: The verse begins with a plural, "they rebuilt," and ends with a singular, hēgiasen, "he consecrated." Sinaiticus has the plural (see the variant). Alexandrinus has singulars in 4:47 and 4:57 too ("he took," "he built," "he renewed"), so its text may present Judas as the one who rebuilt and consecrated, with the people working under him. The book does not say who led the worship as high priest (see the note at 4:42).
orig: καὶ τὰς αὐλὰς ἡγίασεν (kai tas aulas hēgiasen)

a: the altar for burnt offerings and incense
p: The Greek lists 'the altar of burnt offerings and of incense.' The Temple had two altars.
b: The burnt offering altar stood in the courtyard and had just been rebuilt (4:47); the incense altar stood inside, with the lampstand and table (Exodus 30:1–6; 40:5). The Greek to thysiastērion tōn holokautōmatōn kai thymiamatōn seems to run the two together, and the burnt offering altar would hardly be "brought into the Temple." Most interpreters think the incense altar is meant, or that a Hebrew "altar of incense" was expanded. Antiochus had taken away the golden altar (1:21).
orig: τὸ θυσιαστήριον τῶν ὁλοκαυτωμάτων καὶ θυμιαμάτων (to thysiastērion tōn holokautōmatōn kai thymiamatōn)

a: lit the lamps of the lampstand, and light shone in the Temple
p: The law commanded the lamps to burn always. Later tradition made the light the heart of Hanukkah.
b: Aaron was to keep the lamps in order before the LORD "always" (Leviticus 24:2–4), and the bread set out every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9; 4:51). 1 Maccabees tells of lighting the lamps but not of any miracle. The Babylonian Talmud's story of a single jar of pure oil that burned for eight days comes centuries later (Shabbat 21b), and Josephus already calls the feast "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325).

a: on the twenty-fifth day of the ninth month, the month of Kislev, in the year 148
p: Three years to the day after the pagan sacrifice of 1:59, in December 164 BC.
b: The year 148 of the Seleucid era, by the reckoning most scholars think 1 Maccabees uses for Temple events (from spring 311 BC), puts the rededication in December 164 BC. The altar had been profaned on 25 Kislev of 145 (1:54, 59), so the book stresses "the same day" (4:54). 2 Maccabees 10:3 counts two years of desecration rather than three. Daniel's numbers, "time, times and half a time" and 1,290 days (Daniel 7:25; 12:7, 11), give about three and a half years, a period that some think counts from earlier events in 168/167 BC.

a: with songs and harps and lyres and cymbals
p: As at Solomon's Temple and Nehemiah's walls, the Levites' instruments sound at the dedication.
b: David appointed Levites to play "lyres, harps and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 15:16; 25:1); they played when the ark entered Solomon's Temple (2 Chronicles 5:12–13), and Nehemiah brought them to dedicate the walls "with thanksgiving songs and singing, with cymbals, lyres and harps" (Nehemiah 12:27). The music silenced in 3:45 returns.

a: for eight days
p: Solomon's dedication and Hezekiah's cleansing lasted eight days; 2 Maccabees links the feast to Booths.
b: Solomon kept the dedication of the altar for seven days and the feast seven more, with an assembly on the eighth (2 Chronicles 7:8–9); Hezekiah's priests finished their cleansing on the eighth day (2 Chronicles 29:17); and the Feast of Booths has eight days (Leviticus 23:36). 2 Maccabees 10:6 says the people kept eight days "as one keeps the Feast of Booths," remembering that they had spent Booths in the mountains like wild animals, and the letter at the book's opening tells the Jews of Egypt to "keep the days of the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev" (2 Maccabees 1:9).

a: offerings of praise
p: The Greek thysia aineseōs is the Septuagint's term for the thank offering of Leviticus 7.
b: The thank offering (todah) was a kind of peace offering eaten by the worshiper (Leviticus 7:12–15). Psalm 50:14 says, "Sacrifice a thank offering to God," and Hebrews 13:15 takes the phrase up: "let us offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, the fruit of lips."
orig: θυσίαν σωτηρίου καὶ αἰνέσεως (thysian sōtēriou kai aineseōs)

a: gold crowns and little shields
p: Ornaments on the Temple's front, replacing those Antiochus had stripped (1:22).
b: Antiochus had taken "the gold decoration on the front of the Temple" (1:22). Votive crowns and shields hung on temples across the Greek world; Solomon made golden shields for his palace (1 Kings 10:16–17), and Zechariah's crowns were laid up in the Temple as a memorial (Zechariah 6:14). The Mishnah mentions golden chains and crowns on the Temple's porch (Mishnah Middot 3:8).

a: the days of the dedication of the altar should be kept at their season every year
p: The origin of Hanukkah ('Dedication'), the feast Jesus attended in John 10:22.
b:
The feast was set by the people's assembly, not by the law of Moses, and so it is not one of the feasts of Leviticus 23. Its name comes from the older dedications: Numbers uses the same phrase, "the dedication of the altar" (Greek enkainismos tou thysiastēriou), for the leaders' offerings when the Tabernacle altar was anointed (Numbers 7:10–11, 84–88); Solomon and all Israel "dedicated the LORD's house" (1 Kings 8:63); and the title of Psalm 30, "A song for the dedication of the house," has long been read at Hanukkah. John 10:22–23 says, "The Feast of Dedication came around in Jerusalem. It was wintertime, and Jesus was walking around in the temple, in Solomon's Porch." Josephus says the feast was kept in his day and called "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325). 2 Maccabees opens with letters urging Egyptian Jews to keep it (2 Maccabees 1:9, 18).

The rabbis kept the feast but not the book: the Mishnah mentions Hanukkah only in passing, and the Babylonian Talmud centers it on the miracle of the oil (Shabbat 21b). On whether churches may set up feasts the law does not command, see the card on the chapter page.
orig: ἄγωνται ἡμέραι ἐγκαινισμοῦ τοῦ θυσιαστηρίου (agōntai hēmerai enkainismou tou thysiastēriou)
r: Numbers 7:10–11; Numbers 7:84–88; 1 Kings 8:63–66; Psalm 30:1; John 10:22–23; 2 Maccabees 1:9; 2 Maccabees 1:18; Esther 9:20–28

a: they built high walls and strong towers around Mount Zion
p: Here 'Mount Zion' means the Temple mount, facing the Seleucid Citadel across the city.
b: In 1 Maccabees "Mount Zion" is the Temple hill (4:37; 5:54; 7:33), not the western hill that later took the name. The fortified Temple faced the Citadel (1:33), whose garrison would harass the worshipers for twenty years, until Simon took it in 141 BC (13:49–52). The walls were pulled down by the young king Antiochus V (6:62).
